extracted.intended_audience: creative writers (students, MFA candidates, short-story authors) working on revision and thematic cohesion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for revising and assembling short stories into a thematically coherent collection, focusing on characterization, point of view, endings, and psychological realism. Emphasizes concrete revision choices made to strengthen resonance and avoid caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the 'Why' (motivation) for characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and make clear why a character behaves as they do — e.g., 'the question of why this man was so obsessed with the lake always came up.' Without the 'Why,' the story can read as a mere character sketch or anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a motive that gives the piece resonance with readers and explains why key events (like Jimmy's removal from the lake) are significant. Use backstory or concrete incidents (e.g., James' death by encephalitis) to root behavior in cause and consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings must fit the character's established limits and psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the resolution or ending follows from the character as written; don't force actions that conflict with established traits — author changed ending so Jimmy is taken rather than voluntarily leaving because voluntary departure 'was not fitting with his character.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When revising endings, test whether the character would plausibly choose the action you give them; if not, alter the ending to maintain psychological truth. Example: changing a voluntary leave into being 'taken from the lake' to preserve Jimmy's obsessive attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic coherence across a collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a recurring thematic concern (here, obsession) to connect stories in a collection: 'This piece’s thematic focus on obsession represents a connection between “Jimmy of the Lake” and two other stories in this collection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make deliberate thematic choices so individual pieces resonate together. Rework or select stories so shared motifs and concerns (obsession, fantasy, self-delusion) appear in multiple pieces without redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat obsession as complex and ambivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray obsession as both potential strength and weakness — 'Obsession is an important thematic concern ... it can be both a positive and negative character trait.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one-dimensional depictions; show how obsession fuels achievement or identity as well as self-destruction. Use varied examples (historical figures, characters) to illustrate nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and control point of view to shape reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use unreliable first-person narrators intentionally: 'I use first-person and attempt to apply some of what I have learned about unreliable first-person narrator’s ...' and 'I use the points of view of other characters to contrast with the narrator’s point of view and show how his perspective is skewed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to make the narrator reliable or unreliable and use contrasting perspectives (other characters' POVs) to reveal discrepancies. Use unreliability to create psychological realism and layered meaning rather than confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the unreliable narrator to hide the author’s hand and increase suspension of disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: The unreliable narrator can 'hide the hand of the author, increase the ability for the reader to suspend disbelief and still communicate with the reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply unreliability strategically to withhold or distort information, letting readers infer truths while maintaining narrative plausibility. Don't use unreliability as a gimmick—ensure it serves psychological realism or thematic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to reconstruct plot radically while preserving character voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision may require discarding early plotlines and building a new plot around a surviving core (e.g., only the main character and voice remained from the original draft of 'Ninth Texas Calvary').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a draft's plot isn't working, retain what is strongest (character, voice) and rebuild the story. Radical reconstruction is acceptable when it strengthens coherence and avoids forced elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid caricature by selecting believable obsessions and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character has an extreme trait (e.g., doomsday prepping), choose the form of obsession that can be portrayed credibly and avoid making them a caricature — the author 'chose to focus on battle re-enactment because ... it was easier to portray a character obsessed ... and keep the character from becoming a caricature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which traits invite empathy or credibility. If an obsession risks caricature, shift emphasis to aspects that allow nuance (ritual, longing, identity) rather than spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base characters on real people but let fiction reshape them
rubrics_metrics.description: Use real-life acquaintances as inspiration ('The character Larry is based off of a friend of my father’s') but allow the fictional character to diverge as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on real details to add specificity, but change events, motivations, and outcomes to serve the story, not strict verisimilitude or memoir constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory detail and setting to immerse readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rich sensory description (e.g., shells 'made a sound like pebbles trickling through a rainstick,' 'the orange sliver of sun') grounds the scene and evokes atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor scenes in tactile, auditory, olfactory, and visual details to create immediacy. Let setting reveal character (Jimmy's comfort at the lake vs. the house) and theme (lake as locus of obsession and memory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Root character behavior in backstory and loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain obsessive behavior through formative events (Jimmy's son's death, brother's wartime death) so actions feel motivated: 'After James’ death ... he started camping out down by the lake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific losses or traumas as causal anchors for present behavior rather than vague assertions. Show rather than tell: reveal how memory, rituals, and environment sustain an obsession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore psychological realism and the boundary with mental illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to 'make stories more psychological realistic' and 'pressure the boundary between sanity and mental illness' by conveying thought patterns typical of various conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and depict cognitive patterns, obsessions, and compulsions with nuance and empathy. Avoid stigmatizing language; render interiority in ways that help readers understand thought processes and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use character relationships to expose fault lines in worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpersonal dynamics (e.g., Larry and Dana) should challenge and reveal the obsessive character's limits: 'Dana challenges the narrator to acknowledge the futility of his obsession with control and order.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce characters who resist or complicate the protagonist’s worldview so conflicts reveal internal stakes and force change or reveal tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select which obsessions to foreground during revision
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character exhibits multiple obsessions (e.g., doomsday prepping vs. battle re-enactment), decide which to foreground for narrative clarity and depth: 'I chose to focus on battle re-enactment because I felt that it was easier to portray a character obsessed ... and keep the character from becoming a caricature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In revision, pare competing obsessions down to the ones that best serve character development and thematic focus. Use secondary obsessions only if they complicate rather than distract.
